analysis:
All three changed files are offline CI test scripts, covering scripts/test-ci-component-paths.py, scripts/test-cluster-test-plan.py and scripts/test-darkbloom-route.py. None touches provider runtime code, keys, attestation, the coordinator WebSocket, the prefix cache or any other threat-model asset.

The changes update test assertions so CI macOS jobs (test-provider, test-provider-summary, test-provider-sdk, test-cluster-checks, test-cluster, test-cluster-gpu, test-cluster-focused) route through the darkbloom-route plane. Previously they used a literal Blacksmith label. Each job now declares `needs: [changes, route]`. Sharded jobs request per-shard lanes named `<job>-<shard>`, with fallback labels.

The tests still check security-relevant workflow invariants. These include no secrets, no id-token, no environment and no cross-repository checkout in ci.yml, component-changes.yml and provider-release-cache.yml. Release and credentialed workflows keep literal runners (the UNROUTED list and its test). The route job has `permissions: {}` and no secrets. The classifier uses full history and has no pull_request_target. The provider-test-gate truth table is unchanged.

One test (test_release_and_credentialed_workflows_keep_literal_runners) loses its CI_MACOS_JOBS literal-runner assertion. That assertion is replaced by routing assertions, and those jobs are non-credentialed PR-test lanes. I saw no secret or release exposure.

The real workflow files (ci.yml, darkbloom-route.yml) are not in this batch. Whether the routed runner labels can be influenced by fork PRs, or whether a fallback label could run untrusted code on a privileged self-hosted runner, is therefore unverified. Any such concern is outside the supplied evidence, and I am not raising it as a finding. No threat IDs are implicated by these test-only edits. An integration pass could check the actual ci.yml route job against these expectations.
